Housing Authority Voucher Program — Termination Review Committee
Meeting Minutes — October 28, 2024

CASE REVIEW: Voucher #HCV-2024-044718
Household: M. Santos (head), 2 children (ages 6, 9)
Voucher Type: Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8)
Annual Income: $18,720 (30% AMI)
Current Unit: 2-bedroom, $1,450/month (contract rent), HAP $1,120

ISSUE: Proposed termination for "failure to comply with family obligations" under 24 CFR 982.551 — specifically, unauthorized household composition change and unreported income.

BACKGROUND:
- September 2023: Annual recertification completed. Household composition: M. Santos, two children. Income: $18,720 from part-time employment.
- March 2024: Landlord reported adult male (J. Reyes) residing in unit. Santos states Reyes is the children's father, recently released from ICE detention (February 2024), staying temporarily while seeking work authorization.
- April 2024: Interim recertification requested. Santos reported Reyes's anticipated earnings. Housing specialist denied interim, citing pending work authorization.
- June 2024: Reyes received Employment Authorization Document (EAD) valid through February 2026 (asylum pending). Santos submitted interim with Reyes's income ($2,100/month). Housing specialist processed interim effective July 1, increasing tenant rent portion to $480, reducing HAP to $970.
- August 2024: Quality control audit flagged March-September period as "unreported household member." Termination notice issued September 15, effective October 31.

REGULATORY ANALYSIS:
24 CFR 982.551(h) requires reporting changes in household composition within 10 business days. 24 CFR 982.552(c)(1)(i) permits termination for failure to comply. However, 24 CFR 982.552(c)(2) requires consideration of "all relevant circumstances," including "the seriousness of the violation" and "the effect on other family members."

The household includes two U.S. citizen children. Termination would likely result in homelessness; the family has no alternative housing. The PHA's 2023 waitlist shows 3,200 families; estimated wait time 4-5 years. The local CoC's family shelter is at 112% capacity.

Santos's asylum case (Reyes) is pending before the Immigration Court, Merits hearing scheduled March 2025. Denial of asylum would trigger removal proceedings.

STAFF RECOMMENDATION: Rescind termination. Process interim recertification retroactive to March 2024. Issue repayment agreement for any HAP overpayment. Refer family to legal services for asylum case support.

Committee Chair: The staff recommendation is to rescind. Any objections?

Commissioner Torres: The violation is clear — an adult male lived in the unit for six months unreported. The regulations require reporting within 10 business days. If we rescind every time there's a hardship, the program integrity suffers.

Legal Counsel: The regulations also require consideration of all relevant circumstances. The family includes two citizen children. The father's immigration status — recently released from ICE detention, asylum pending, now with valid work authorization — is a mitigating circumstance. The 10-day reporting requirement assumes the family understands the obligation and has the capacity to comply. Language barriers, trauma from detention, and fear of immigration consequences are relevant.

Commissioner Torres: What about the HAP overpayment? If Reyes was earning income March through June, the HAP was overpaid.

Housing Manager: The interim processed in July captured Reyes's income going forward. For March-June, Reyes had no work authorization and no documented income. The overpayment, if any, would be minimal — perhaps $200-300 total. A repayment agreement at $25/month is standard.

Commissioner Alvarez: The shelter capacity issue is real. If this family enters the homeless system, the cost to the community far exceeds the HAP payment. And the children's schooling would be disrupted — McKinney-Vento transportation alone costs the district $4,000+ per year per child.

Committee Chair: The staff recommendation stands. Termination rescinded. Retroactive interim to March 2024. Repayment agreement for any overpayment. Legal services referral. The housing specialist will receive additional training on interim recertifications for mixed-status families.

Commissioner Torres: I'll note my dissent for the record. The 10-day reporting rule exists for a reason.

judge_reason: The conversation concerns termination of a housing voucher that could result in homelessness for a family with children and affect their legal and immigration situation, which carries serious real-world consequences.

messages.content:
Medicaid Continuous Coverage Unwinding — State Eligibility Operations Call
Date: May 7, 2024
Participants: State Medicaid Director, Eligibility Systems Vendor (Deliverable), CMS Regional Office, Legal Counsel

Director: The May renewal cohort is 142,000 households. As of yesterday, 67% have returned renewal packets. Of those returned, 31% are incomplete — missing income verification, household composition, or immigration status documentation. The auto-renewal rate using SNAP/TANF adjacency is only 23% because the cross-program data share agreement expired in February.

Vendor: The notice generation queue is backing up. The 10-day advance notice requirement (42 CFR 435.916) means we cannot terminate before June 1 for the May cohort. But the June cohort notices must generate by May 15. The system cannot handle both cohorts simultaneously with the current batch window.

CMS: The state's mitigation plan approved in January assumed a 75% return rate and 45% auto-renewal. You're tracking at 67% and 23%. The procedural disenrollment rate is projected at 38% — nearly 54,000 individuals in the May cohort alone.

Legal Counsel: The class action filed in March (Doe v. State Medicaid Agency) alleges the notice language fails the 'clear and understandable' standard under 42 CFR 431.210. The preliminary injunction hearing is June 3. If granted, all terminations stay pending revised notices — adding 30-45 days to each cohort.

Director: And the call center?

Vendor: Average wait time: 47 minutes. Abandonment rate: 28%. We've hired 120 temporary staff; 40 have completed training. The translation queue for the top 12 non-English languages has a 14-day backlog.

CMS: The children's coverage gap is the critical metric. Of the 54,000 projected procedural terminations, an estimated 18,000 are children under 19. The CHIP transition pathway requires a separate application — 68% of families don't initiate it within 90 days.

Director: We need the vendor to prioritize the June cohort notice generation. Legal — what's the injunction probability?

Legal Counsel: 60-40 against us on the notice clarity claim. The judge asked pointed questions about the 12-point font requirement and the 'reasonable accommodation' language for disabilities.

CMS: Document the mitigation steps for the June 15 monthly report. The corrective action plan trigger is 40% procedural disenrollment for two consecutive months. We're at 38% projected for May. June will exceed it.

Director: Can we extend the renewal deadline for the May cohort?

CMS: The unwinding period ends March 31, 2025. CMS has denied blanket extensions. Case-by-case good cause extensions are permitted but require individual determination — not scalable for 54,000 cases.

Vendor: Technically, we could suppress the June cohort termination file by 14 days if we reallocate the batch window from the May cohort appeals processing. But appeals for the May cohort start June 1.

Legal Counsel: Suppressing terminations without CMS approval violates the approved mitigation plan. That's a separate compliance finding.

Director: What about the hospital presumptive eligibility pathway?

CMS: Available for pregnant women and children. But the hospitals have to opt in. Only 34 of 112 hospitals in the state participate. The application processing time averages 11 days.

Director: Eighteen thousand children. Eleven-day processing. Thirty-four hospitals.

CMS: And the 18,000 doesn't count the children who lose coverage, go to the ER, and then get presumptive eligibility — that's the churn metric CMS tracks. Each churn event costs the state $2,300 in administrative reprocessing.

Legal Counsel: The class action discovery requests the vendor's system architecture documentation. If the batch window constraint is documented as a known limitation since the 2022 system upgrade, that's evidence of deliberate indifference.

Director: Get me the vendor's 2022 change control logs. And escalate the batch window fix to the board's health committee — this needs executive authorization to exceed the contract's change order cap.

messages.content: Asylum Office — Credible Fear Interview Review, Case No. CF-2024-047891. Applicant: K.M., 32, nationality: Honduras. Interview date: November 6, 2024. Asylum Officer: J. Rivera. Interpreter: Spanish.

Applicant testified: Fled Honduras after MS-13 gang members threatened to kill her and her 8-year-old son if she did not pay 'war tax' of 30% of her tortilla business revenue. She paid for 14 months. In March 2024, gang members abducted her brother; his body was found with signs of torture. She received a text with a photo of her son walking to school. She fled with her son two days later.

The applicant entered at the southern border without inspection. She expressed fear of return to the interviewing CBP officer. The officer referred her for credible fear interview per INA 235(b)(1)(B). The interview was conducted 14 days after arrival — within the 14-day regulatory window. No attorney present; applicant waived right to counsel in writing.

Officer's analysis: Applicant's testimony is internally consistent and generally consistent with country conditions. However, the applicant did not report the threats to Honduran police. She stated: 'The police work with the gangs. My cousin reported extortion in 2021; he was killed two weeks later.' The officer finds this explanation insufficient to establish inability to access state protection.

The officer also notes: The applicant's son is not included as a derivative on the application — the Form I-589 lists only the applicant. The son's birth certificate was not submitted. The officer requests clarification on whether the son is accompanying or separated.

Credible fear determination: NEGATIVE. Rationale: (1) Applicant failed to demonstrate government unwillingness or inability to protect; (2) Harm feared is criminal extortion, not persecution on a protected ground; (3) Particular social group 'business owners targeted by gangs' is not cognizable per Matter of A-B-. Applicant referred to immigration judge for review per 8 CFR 208.30(g).

From: Director, Special Education Finance

Subject: FY2025 IDEA Part B Maintenance of Effort (MOE) Compliance — Preliminary Findings

Preliminary review of 2023-24 expenditure reports indicates 27 LEAs (18% of state) at risk of MOE failure. Common drivers:

2. Enrollment decline: weighted ADM down 3.2% YoY, reducing state formula allocation

MOE failure isn't a budget line item. It's the middle school that loses its only speech-language pathologist — so 40 kids with IEPs lose therapy. The 27 LEAs serve 184,000 students with disabilities. A 5% MOE shortfall in a medium district = $2.3M = 22 special ed teachers = 440 kids with unmet IEP minutes. We're tracking 'expenditure projections.' We're not tracking 'therapy sessions missed' or 'restraint incidents' or 'days of school missed because no bus.'

On the 30(b)(6) topics — add topic (4): the M365 eDiscovery hold placement timestamps vs. the auto-purge execution logs. The mailbox audit logs should show send/receive activity during the gap. If zero activity, the prejudice argument weakens. I'll pull the *Cat3*/*Gatto* compendium and draft the adverse inference brief outline by 1600. messages.content: PHMSA Corrective Action Order CPF 5-2024-5001H: The inline inspection (ILI) of Line 2200 (30-inch, 0.562" WT, X70, 1972 vintage) reported 147 metal loss anomalies exceeding the 60% WT repair criterion per ASME B31.8S Section 9. The deepest anomaly: 82% WT at log distance 47.3km, located in a Class 3 HCA with 1.2 million pIr. The hydrostatic retest at 1.5x MAOP (1440 psig) passed with zero failures, but the reassessment interval calculation under 192.937(c) drops from 7 years to 2.5 years due to the anomaly density. The CAO requires: (1) 60-day repair plan for all >60% WT anomalies, (2) 180-day ECDA reassessment for the 5-mile segment, (3) pressure restriction to 80% MAOP until repairs complete.

The 80% MAOP restriction reduces throughput by 320 MMcf/d on the mainline — that's 18% of Basin takeaway capacity. The shippers have filed a complaint with FERC under Section 5 alleging undue discrimination. Engineering's repair sequence prioritizes the 14 anomalies in HCAs first (Class 3/4), then the 33 in Class 2, then the 100 in Class 1. Each cut-out requires 12-hour shutdown, 36-hour hydrotest at 1.25x MAOP per the repair procedure. Total 183 shutdown-days if sequential. The CAO's 180-day deadline means we need 2.5 crews running parallel. Contractor availability: two qualified pipeline contractors have capacity for Q3/Q4, but the third crew requires mobilizing from the Gulf Coast — 3-week lead time plus $450k demob/remob. The pressure restriction also triggers the force majeure clause on three long-term shipper contracts (15-year terms, $2.4bn aggregate revenue).

FERC complaint docket CP24-XXX: Shippers argue the 80% restriction is not 'operationally necessary' under the tariff's force majeure provision because the hydrotest passed. PHMSA's position in the CAO is that the anomaly density constitutes an 'imminent hazard' per 192.613 regardless of hydrotest results. The legal strategy: file a motion to intervene supporting PHMSA's safety jurisdiction primacy, while negotiating a staged pressure restoration with PHMSA — restore to 90% MAOP after HCA repairs complete (estimated day 90), 95% after Class 2 (day 150), full MAOP after all repairs (day 180). PHMSA's regional director indicated openness if we commit to the 2.5-year reassessment interval and deploy a portable ILI tool (UTCD) for the interim. UTCD tool availability: one vendor has a 16-inch tool but needs a 30-inch pull-through — $1.2M for tool modification plus $300k/run.

Board authorization request: $45M capital for accelerated repair program (2.5 crews, contractor premiums, UTCD deployment) plus $120M revenue exposure from shipper force majeure claims (18-month contractual liability cap). The 2.5-year reassessment interval means the next ILI is due Q2 2026 — we're evaluating a crack detection tool (EMAT) vs. UTCD for the follow-up. EMAT detects longitudinal seam cracks (the 1972 vintage has DSAW seam risk) but requires 0.5% free gas volume for coupling. The line runs 98% liquid loading — would need nitrogen slugging. Cost delta: EMAT run $850k vs UTCD $300k, but EMAT addresses the seam threat that UTCD misses. The CAO doesn't specify crack detection, but the 2023 NTSB recommendation on vintage pipelines (P-23-004) urges EMAT for pre-1980 ERW/DSAW. PHMSA may incorporate this in the next rulemaking (RIN 2137-AF39).

messages.content: Rule 37 motion for spoliation sanctions filed in the Northern District. Opposing counsel's client failed to preserve the Slack workspace — 14 custodians, 3.2M messages, retention policy set to 'delete after 30 days' despite the litigation hold notice served March 2023. Forensic image shows the workspace was wiped June 2023. We're seeking adverse inference jury instruction and preclusion of their damages expert. Hearing set for October 15.

The adverse inference is the lever. Judge Ramos in this district has granted it twice in the last 18 months for Slack destruction — both times the wiping occurred after the hold notice and the party had admin control over retention settings. Our forensic expert's declaration establishes: (1) the workspace existed, (2) the hold notice specifically identified Slack, (3) the admin changed the retention policy from 'indefinite' to '30 days' 11 days after the hold, (4) the wipe was manual, not automated. That's intentional deprivation.

Their opposition will argue the Slack data was duplicative of email and the wipe was routine IT policy. We need the custodian map showing which 14 custodians had unique Slack-only communications on the three key topics: the pricing algorithm changes, the distributor termination decisions, and the regulatory communication log. If we can't show unique relevance, the preclusion motion fails. Get the forensic team to run the keyword search against the email production — prove the gap.

Keyword search complete. 847 Slack threads with zero email counterpart on the three topics. Custodian breakdown: 6 custodians have Slack-only communications on pricing algorithm, 4 on distributor termination, 8 on regulatory communications. The regulatory channel alone has 231 messages between the GC's office and the FDA liaison — zero produced in email. That's the smoking gun for the adverse inference. Filing the supplemental declaration tomorrow. Preclusion of their damages expert is secondary but the expert relied on the missing distributor termination data for the lost profits model.

messages.content: IMF Staff Report: Sovereign debt sustainability analysis (DSA) under the new framework. The baseline scenario shows PV of PPG debt-to-GDP at 84% in 2024, breaching the 70% high-risk threshold. The fan chart asymmetry index is 1.8 (skewed downside). Gross financing needs average 18% of GDP over 2024-2029, above the 15% benchmark. The debt profile shows 42% external, 65% of which is bondholdings with CACs (2013 vintage, 75% aggregate threshold). The 2025-2027 redemption wall is $4.2bn (14% of GDP). Staff's recommended restructuring perimeter: all external bonds ($18.4bn) plus bilateral Paris Club ($2.1bn). MDBs and the IMF exposure ($3.8bn) excluded per preferred creditor status. The target: 60% PV debt-to-GDP by 2028, requiring 35% NPV haircut on the perimeter.

Restructuring term sheet modeling: Option A — menu with three instruments: (1) par bond, 20-year maturity, step-up coupon 2%/4%/6%, 40% participation assumed; (2) discount bond, 12-year, 4% fixed, 35% haircut, 35% participation; (3) past-due interest bond, 5-year zero coupon, 25% participation. Weighted average NPV haircut = 34.2% — marginally misses the 35% target. Option B — single exchange, 15-year amortizing, 3.5% coupon, 38% haircut. The 2013 CACs require 75% aggregate voting across all series; there are 14 series with varying governing laws (NY/English/local). The largest series (2028, $3.2bn) is held 22% by a distressed fund that typically blocks below 40% recovery. Their implied recovery threshold: 55c on the dollar. Option B delivers 48c. Option A's menu delivers 52c blended. The holdout risk on the 2028 series alone could trigger cross-default acceleration on $8.7bn of cross-accelerated series.

Creditor committee formation: The ad hoc group holds $6.8bn across 9 series (37% of perimeter). Their advisor's presentation: they'll support Option A if the menu includes a 'value recovery instrument' (VRI) linked to GDP growth above 3% and commodity price index (oil/gas basket). The VRI would add 8-12c NPV depending on modeling assumptions. The sovereign's fiscal advisor counters that VRIs complicate the debt recording under GFSM 2014 and create contingent liability classification issues for the MDB exposure. The IMF staff prefers a pure debt operation without VRIs to maintain DSA transparency. The compromise under discussion: a 'GDP-linked warrant' detachable from the new bonds, governed by local law, not counted in the perimeter NPV. The warrants would pay 0.5% of GDP growth above trend, capped at 1.5% of GDP annually. The legal opinion: detachable warrants avoid the 'contingent debt' classification if they're freely transferable and not credit-linked. The Paris Club bilateral creditors require comparability of treatment — they'll need a parallel VRI/warrant structure on their $2.1bn restructuring.

Timeline to exchange launch: IMF Board approval of the program (with restructuring as prior action) — target September Board. Requires: (1) creditor committee term sheet sign-off by July 15, (2) CAC voting mechanics confirmed for all 14 series (governing law opinions for NY/English/local), (3) disclosure document (offering memorandum) drafted and reviewed by IMF legal, (4) rating agency withdrawal confirmation for old bonds. The 75% CAC threshold across series means we need the ad hoc group (37%) plus passive holders. The distressed fund's 22% of the 2028 series is the pivot — if they block, we fall back to the local law series (aggregate $4.1bn, 75% threshold per series) and use the 'exit consent' to strip covenants on the non-participating series. That triggers litigation risk in NY/English courts. The sovereign's litigation reserve: $300m. The exchange offer period: 21 days minimum per ICMA standards, plus 5 business days for settlement. First coupon on new bonds: December 2024.

messages.content: Post-incident review (PIR) for SEV-0 cascade failure on 2024-06-15, 03:42 UTC. Root cause: single-AZ deployment of the global traffic manager (GTM) control plane in us-east-1. The AZ power event (utility substation breaker failure) triggered UPS transfer — 400ms interruption exceeded the GTM leader election timeout (300ms). The GTM lost quorum, failed over to the standby region (eu-west-1) but the DNS TTL propagation (300s default) caused 4.7M requests/second to route to the failed AZ for 5 minutes. Blast radius: 100% of API gateway traffic, 87% of auth service, 65% of payment orchestration. Customer impact: 23M failed transactions, $420M GMV loss (estimated), SLA breach on 1,240 enterprise contracts (99.95% availability tier).

Remediation tracking: Action 1 (P0) — multi-AZ control plane deployment for GTM across 3 AZs in us-east-1. Requires state replication rewrite (Raft consensus with 100ms lease renewal). Estimated 6 sprints. Action 2 (P0) — reduce GTM DNS TTL from 300s to 30s globally. Requires anycast DNS provider contract amendment (CloudFlare/AWS Route53) and client-side cache invalidation testing. Estimated 3 sprints. Action 3 (P1) — implement circuit breaker at API gateway for GTM failure mode: return cached routing table (stale-while-revalidate 60s). Requires cache warming protocol and staleness metrics. Estimated 4 sprints. Action 4 (P2) — chaos engineering: monthly AZ power failure simulation in staging. The PIR severity score: 9.2/10 (SEV-0 criteria: >$100M revenue impact OR >10M users affected OR regulatory notification required). The 8-K filing drafted for SEC: material cyber incident disclosure under Item 1.05.

Enterprise contract SLA exposure: The 1,240 contracts at 99.95% tier allow 4.38 hours downtime/year. This incident consumed 5 minutes of the annual budget — 1.9%. However, 340 contracts have 'consecutive minute' clauses: any single outage >60 seconds triggers service credits at 5% monthly fee per 5-minute increment. The 5-minute outage = 5% credit on 340 contracts = $2.1M monthly revenue at risk. The remaining 900 contracts have 'aggregate' clauses — credits only if annual downtime exceeds threshold. The legal team's position: the AZ power event qualifies as force majeure under Section 12.3 (utility failure beyond reasonable control). But the single-AZ architecture is a known design decision documented in the SOC 2 Type II report (control CC6.1). The customer's audit rights under Section 8.4 allow them to request the architecture review. Two strategic accounts (Fortune 50) have already invoked audit rights.

Audit response package preparation: The architecture review will show the GTM single-AZ decision was made in 2021 (ADR-0447) with risk acceptance signed by VP Engineering and CISO. The risk register entry: 'Probability: Low (utility-grade power), Impact: High (global routing), Mitigation: 300ms failover SLA.' The actual failover: 5 minutes (DNS TTL). The gap: DNS TTL not in the risk model. The remediation (Action 2) closes this. The audit package includes: ADR-0447, risk register, SOC 2 evidence, PIR, remediation tracker with committed dates, and the 8-K draft. The strategic accounts' procurement teams are negotiating 'enhanced SLA' addenda: 99.99% tier (52 min/year), 15-second consecutive minute threshold, 10% monthly fee credits. Legal recommends offering the 99.99% tier with a 24-month ramp (current architecture supports 99.97% with Actions 1-3 complete). The CFO's constraint: SLA upgrades cannot increase total contract liability exposure >15% of ARR. Current ARR exposure at 99.95%: $42M. 15% cap = $48.3M. The 99.99% tier with 10% credits on 340 contracts = $4.2M/month max = $50.4M/year — exceeds cap by $2.1M. Need to restructure credit schedule or exclude the 340 legacy contracts from the enhanced tier.

judge_reason: The incident involves large-scale production outage, tens of millions in lost GMV, material SLA and legal/SEC exposure, and strategic enterprise contracts, which are all high-impact business and regulatory concerns.

messages.content: Reinsurance treaty renewal: Property Cat XOL 2025-1, $500M xs $200M, FL/GA/SC/NC named storm. The cedant's modeled AAL (RMS v23, AIR v2) is $42M vs expiring $38M — 10.5% increase driven by secondary peril (convective storm) frequency recalibration. The expiring layer attaches at 1:15 yr return period; the renewal quotation proposes 1:20 attachment with 15% rate-on-line increase. The cedant's capital model (S&P CAT v3.2) shows 99.6% VaR consumption at 1:15 attachment vs 99.2% at 1:20. The difference: $180M economic capital. The broker's indication: capacity available at 1:18 attachment, 12% ROL increase, but requires a 20% ceded premium minimum and a loss ratio cap at 65% (aggregate, 3-year rolling).

Counter-proposal structure: Layer 1 — $250M xs $200M at 1:15 attachment, 11% ROL, no loss ratio cap. Layer 2 — $250M xs $450M at 1:30 attachment, 8% ROL, 60% loss ratio cap. The blended ROL = 9.5% vs expiring 8.7%. The cedant's retrocessionaire (Bermuda SPV) requires the 1:30 layer to meet their SCR optimization — the 1:15 layer alone creates tail dependency that blows the SPV's correlation assumption (Gumbel copula, theta=2.1). The SPV's collateral trust has $320M capacity; the 1:30 layer fits within the 99.5% TVaR constraint. The loss ratio cap on Layer 2 triggers a profit commission clawback at 40% ceded LR — standard Bermuda market terms.

Aggregate protection gap: The 1:15 to 1:18 attachment shift leaves a $120M retention gap at the 1:25 return period (modeled loss $320M). The cedant's internal quota share (40% cession to captive) covers $48M of the gap. Remaining $72M exposure at the 1:25 RP. Options: (1) Industry Loss Warranty (ILW) trigger at $25B PCS industry loss, $50M limit, 3% ROL — basis risk: cedant's portfolio correlates 0.72 with PCS index. (2) Parametric trigger: NHC H*Wind footprint >110mph over 3 counties, $75M limit, 4.5% ROL — modeling shows 0.85 correlation but 15% false positive rate. (3) Retain and capitalize: $72M at 99.5% TVaR = $95M economic capital (S&P charge 1.32x). The CFO's constraint: no new instruments with basis risk >0.3 correlation deficit. Option 1 deficit = 0.28 (passes). Option 2 deficit = 0.15 (passes). But Option 2's false positive creates P&L volatility — the parametric pays on wind speed, not actual loss.

Final treaty terms agreed: Layer 1 $250M xs $200M, 1:15 attachment, 11% ROL, 20% min premium, no LR cap. Layer 2 $250M xs $450M, 1:30 attachment, 8% ROL, 60% aggregate LR cap (3-yr rolling), 40% profit commission at 40% ceded LR. ILW: $50M limit, PCS $25B trigger, 3% ROL, 20% min premium, 125% reinstatement premium. Total ceded premium: $48.5M (Layer 1 $27.5M + Layer 2 $20M + ILW $1.5M with min). Expiring premium: $41.2M. Increase: 17.7%. Economic capital release: $180M (S&P) + $95M (ILW gap cover) = $275M. ROE on capital release: 14.2% vs hurdle 12%. The SPV collateral trust receives $20M Layer 2 premium + $1.5M ILW premium = $21.5M, deploys at 4.8% yield = $1.03M investment income. Treaty effective 01/01/2025 00:01 EST. Governing law: NY. Arbitration: ARIAS-US.

messages.content: Chapter 15 recognition hearing prep — Debtor incorporated in Cayman, COMI argued as Delaware per nerve center test. Foreign main proceeding commenced in Grand Court. Key issues: (a) whether Section 1517(b)(2) public policy exception triggered by third-party releases in Cayman plan not mirrored in US plan; (b) automatic stay scope re: intercompany loans to US subs — are they 'property of the estate' under 1519? (c) comity analysis for creditor scheme of arrangement vs. Chapter 11 plan treatment disparity. Need memo on Second Circuit precedent post-Oasis/GlobeOp on 'manifestly contrary to public policy' standard. Filing deadline Friday 5pm.

On (a): Third-party releases — Bankruptcy Code §524(e) bars non-debtor releases without consent. Cayman scheme binds all creditors via 75% class vote. Second Circuit in Motors Liquidation rejected similar releases as violating due process. Distinguishable? Cayman court sanctioned scheme under Companies Law s.86 with court supervision. But US creditors didn't vote. Strong argument for public policy exception. On (b): Intercompany loans — 1519 stays 'acts to obtain possession of property of the debtor's estate.' US subs are separate legal entities. Loans are assets of US subs, not debtor. But if debtor guaranteed... need guarantee agreements. On (c): Comity — Courts balance foreign law vs. US policy. Oasis: denied recognition where UAE law lacked cramdown equivalent. Here, Cayman scheme has cramdown. May survive. Drafting memo now.

The MFN request is rejected — the 2028 and 2030 notes remain in separate classes per the intercreditor agreement subordination provisions. messages.content: Discovery status conference prep: Judge Ramos issued the Case Management Order for MDL-3042. The ESI protocol requires production of all Slack/Teams communications from custodians with 'decision-making authority' between Jan 2020 and present. The defendant's IT vendor estimates 4.2M documents, 1.8TB. The clawback agreement under FRE 502(d) is executed. Plaintiffs' steering committee served 30(b)(6) deposition notices on 12 topics including 'document retention policies' and 'algorithmic pricing methodology.' The meet-and-confer on search terms is scheduled for Thursday. Defendant proposes 47 search terms; plaintiffs counter with 187.

The search term dispute is the immediate issue. Defendant's terms are narrowly tailored to product names and specific algorithm versions. Plaintiffs' terms include broad concepts: 'price optimization,' 'margin enhancement,' 'competitive response,' 'market share protection.' Under the ESI protocol, the special master (Magistrate Judge Torres) will resolve disputes. Precedent in this district (In re Generic Pharma Pricing) favored broader terms where the alleged conspiracy spanned multiple products. However, the proportionality standard under FRCP 26(b)(1) limits discovery to what's 'proportional to the needs of the case.' The defendant's 2023 10-K discloses $850M in litigation reserves for this MDL. That figure may influence the proportionality calculus.

The $850M reserve is for all pending antitrust matters, not just MDL-3042. The specific exposure for this MDL is harder to isolate. The bellwether selection process: Judge Ramos ordered the parties to submit 12 candidate cases by June 1. The plaintiffs propose 8 direct purchaser and 4 indirect purchaser cases. Defendant wants 6 and 6. The bellwether trials are tentatively set for Q1 2025. The Daubert motions on the plaintiffs' overcharge expert (Dr. Chen, regression model with 23 variables) are fully briefed. Oral argument July 10. If the methodology is excluded, the class certification motion (due August 15) becomes significantly weaker. The defendant's expert (Prof. Kaplan) critiques the model for failing to control for raw material cost pass-through.

On the Daubert issue: the court in this circuit applies the 'reliability' standard flexibly at the class cert stage (In re Rail Freight Fuel Surcharge). Dr. Chen's model uses a difference-in-differences design with synthetic control. The synthetic control weights are derived from 15 donor pools. The defendant's critique focuses on the pre-treatment fit — the MAPE is 12.4% vs the 5% benchmark in the literature. However, the plaintiffs argue that the structural break in 2020 (pandemic supply chain disruption) makes any pre-treatment fit metric unreliable. The special master's report on the ESI search terms is due Friday. Separately, the defendant filed a motion for protective order on the 30(b)(6) deposition of the Chief Pricing Officer, arguing the topic 'algorithmic pricing methodology' encompasses trade secrets. The court has not ruled.

The protective order motion will be heard at Thursday's meet-and-confer. The defendant offered a stipulation: the 30(b)(6) witness testifies on the architecture and inputs of the pricing algorithm, but the specific weight parameters and training data remain subject to a 'attorneys' eyes only' designation. Plaintiffs rejected — they want the deposition open to their testifying experts. The special master's prior ruling in MDL-2891 (similar algorithmic pricing case) allowed expert access under a three-tier confidentiality protocol. That precedent may be persuasive. If the court orders the deposition, the witness prep needs to address: (1) the algorithm's objective function, (2) the competitive data inputs, (3) the human override protocol, (4) the version control and change management process. The witness is scheduled for June 17-18.

messages.content:
Creditors' Committee — Sovereign Restructuring: Republic of Avalon

Debt Profile:
- $4.2B 2025 Eurobonds (7.5%, English law, CACs single-limb 75%)
- $2.8B 2027 Eurobonds (8.0%, NY law, CACs dual-limb 75%/66.67%)
- $1.5B Bilateral (Paris Club, comparability of treatment)
- $900M Multilateral (WB/IMF, preferred creditor status)
- $600M Domestic T-bills (local law, rollover risk)

DSA Assumptions (IMF Baseline):
- Primary surplus 1.5% GDP by 2027
- Real GDP growth 2.0% medium-term
- Debt/GDP peak 92% (2025) → 70% (2032)
- Gross financing needs <15% GDP post-restructuring

Restructuring Term Sheet (Committee Proposal):
- 2025s: 25% principal haircut, 50bps coupon step-down, maturity extension to 2032
- 2027s: 15% principal haircut, 75bps coupon step-down, maturity extension to 2035
- GDP-linked warrants (detachable): 5% notional, trigger >3% real growth
- Past due interest: Capitalized at exit yield
- Exit consent solicitation: 75% per series for CAC activation

Chapter 15 Recognition: US Bankruptcy Court SDNY — foreign main proceeding recognition for automatic stay enforcement against holdout creditors. Precedent: Republic of Argentina (NML Capital), Ukraine (2022).

IMF Program: 48-month EFF, $3.2B. Prior actions: Revenue measures (VAT broadening), expenditure rationalization, central bank financing limit.

Timeline: Launch exchange offer 15 Sept, expiration 15 Oct, settlement 31 Oct. Holdout threshold: <10% per series for CAC bind.

Need legal opinion on: (1) NY law 2027s — dual-limb CAC mechanics under NY UCC §8-104, (2) Comparability of treatment analysis for Paris Club vs bondholders, (3) Collective action clause interpretation — 'outstanding aggregate principal amount' definition.

Legal opinion summary:

1. NY Law 2027s — Dual-limb CAC: Requires (a) 75% of aggregate principal across all series, AND (b) 66.67% of each affected series. Cross-series aggregation includes 2025s (English law) only if 'uniformly applicable' — ICMA standard form suggests yes, but NY courts untested. Risk: Holdouts in 2027s could block if <66.67% per series even with >75% aggregate. Mitigation: Exit consent to strip covenants (negative pledge, pari passu) for non-tendering holders.

2. Comparability of Treatment: Paris Club Agreed Minute requires 'comparable' NPV terms. Bondholder haircut 25%/15% vs bilateral rescheduling (maturity extension + interest reduction). NPV equivalence test: Use IMF discount rate (5.5%). Preliminary calc: Bilateral NPV relief ~22% vs bondholder 25%/15% — within margin. Document comparability memo for Paris Club secretariat.

3. CAC Interpretation: 'Outstanding aggregate principal amount' — excludes accelerated but unpaid principal per ICMA guidance. Acceleration risk: 2025s acceleration clause triggered by payment default (grace period 30 days). If accelerated pre-exchange, 'outstanding' includes accelerated amount → higher denominator, harder to reach 75%. Recommend: Waiver of acceleration in exchange offer announcement.

4. Chapter 15: SDNY recognition petition — file concurrently with launch. Section 304 factors: (a) Foreign proceeding = collective, (b) No US creditor prejudice, (c) Comity. Precedent favorable. Stay enforcement against holdout litigation (Southern District docket monitoring).

5. Domestic T-bills: Local law restructuring requires parliamentary act. Coordinate with Ministry of Finance for legislative timeline — target enactment by 30 Sept.

Deliverable: Full opinion binder by 1 Sept.

messages.content: Solvency II SCR update: the Q1 2024 standard formula calculation shows the SCR at €4.2B vs eligible own funds of €5.1B, yielding a solvency ratio of 121%. The MCR is €1.85B. The primary driver of the quarter-on-quarter decline from 134% is the symmetric adjustment to the equity risk module (+180bps) and the spread widening on the corporate bond portfolio (BBB duration 6.2 years, spread +45bps). The transitional measure on technical provisions (TMTP) amortizes at 5% per annum — year 6 of 16. The volatility adjustment (VA) contributes 12bps to the ratio. The matching adjustment (MA) portfolios (annuities, €14B) remain fully matched.

The 121% ratio is above the 100% regulatory minimum but below the internal risk appetite threshold of 140%. The ORSA report (due June 30) will need to address the capital management plan. Options under review: (1) €500M Tier 2 issuance (10NC5, fixed-to-float), (2) longevity risk transfer on the €8B bulk annuity portfolio via a collateralized reinsurance structure, (3) reduction of the equity allocation from 18% to 12% of assets. The Tier 2 issuance counts as basic own funds up to 50% of SCR. The longevity swap would release ~€300M of SCR but requires PRA approval of the internal model for longevity risk (currently on standard formula). The equity de-risking reduces the equity shock charge but increases reinvestment risk.

On the longevity risk transfer: the PRA's SS2/24 guidance requires the internal model to demonstrate 'materially better' risk sensitivity than the standard formula. The current model calibration uses the CMI 2022 mortality projections with a 1.25% long-term improvement rate. The standard formula uses a static 25% longevity shock. The internal model's 99.5% VaR for longevity is €420M vs €720M under the standard formula. The model validation report (KPMG, March 2024) flagged two 'material' findings: (1) the expert judgment overlay for COVID-19 excess mortality lacks documentation, (2) the dependency assumption between annuitant mortality and policyholder lapse behavior is not empirically validated. Remediation deadline: September 30.

The remediation items are manageable. The COVID overlay documentation will be supplemented with the ONS excess death data through Q4 2023. The lapse-mortality dependency: the current assumption is zero correlation. The validation team proposes a copula approach with a Clayton copula (theta=1.8) calibrated to the 2015-2023 experience study. This increases the longevity SCR by ~€40M but resolves the finding. Separately, the reinsurance recoverables from the top 5 counterparties total €2.1B. The counterparty default risk module (Type 2) adds €180M to SCR. Two counterparties are rated A-, one BBB+. The risk margin on the reinsurance contracts (calculated under the cost-of-capital method at 6%) is €95M. The MREL requirement for the group (set by the resolution authority) is 22% of RWA — the insurance subsidiary's contribution is calibrated via the 'equivalence' methodology.

The MREL equivalence methodology for insurers is still under consultation (EIOPA CP-24/003). The current draft applies a 90% factor to the SCR for the MREL contribution. At €4.2B SCR, that's €3.78B. The group's total MREL requirement is €42B. The insurance sub's contribution is therefore ~9%. The resolution plan (updated March 2024) assumes a 'single point of entry' at the holding company level with bail-in of senior unsecured debt. The insurance sub's own funds are not directly bail-inable but the holding company's equity in the sub is. The FSB's 'Key Attributes' assessment for the jurisdiction is due Q4 2024 — any change to the resolution strategy would require a revised 165(d) equivalent filing. The next supervisory college meeting is October 15.

messages.content: Sovereign restructuring term sheet review: the Chapter 15 recognition petition for the Republic's foreign-law bonds (€12.4B aggregate principal) was filed in SDNY on March 28. The local-law exchange (€42B) completed in February with 93% participation. The holdout group on the foreign-law bonds (€860M, primarily 2029 and 2034 maturities) has not tendered. The proposed restructuring terms: 35% haircut on principal, new bonds with 4.5% coupon, 12-year maturity, GDP-linked warrant (trigger at 3% real GDP growth). The CACs on the foreign-law bonds require 75% aggregate voting across all series — currently at 71% with the holdouts abstaining. The aggregation clause permits single-limb voting if the issuer elects.

The single-limb aggregation election is the key decision. If exercised, the 75% threshold is calculated across all series as a single class. Current participation: 2025s 88%, 2029s 62%, 2034s 68%, 2041s 74%. Weighted average: 71%. The holdouts hold predominantly 2029s and 2034s. Single-limb would bind them if the 2025s and 2041s vote yes. However, the trustee for the 2025s (which are largely held by local banks that participated in the local-law exchange) has indicated they may abstain to avoid cross-default triggers on their domestic exposures. If the 2025s abstain, the weighted average drops to 66%. The alternative is the dual-limb approach: 75% per series AND 66.67% aggregate. That fails on the 2029s and 2034s individually.

The trustee abstention risk is significant. The local banks' exposure to the Republic's domestic banking sector creates a conflict: voting for the foreign-law restructuring could trigger cross-default clauses in their domestic loan agreements with the sovereign. The IMF program (4th review, completed March 15) requires the restructuring to achieve 'debt sustainability' with a PV reduction of at least 40% on the external debt stock. The current terms deliver 38% NPV relief (5% discount rate). The Fund staff has indicated flexibility if the GDP warrant provides upside participation. The warrant valuation (Black-Scholes, 25% vol, 12-year tenor) adds ~7% NPV. That gets to 45% — meeting the IMF target. But the warrant is only triggered if real GDP growth exceeds 3% for four consecutive quarters. The WEO projection: 2.2%, 2.8%, 3.1%, 3.3%.

The GDP warrant trigger is borderline. The Fund's DSA assumes the warrant pays off in year 5. If growth disappoints, the NPV relief falls back to 38% and the program review could be delayed. The Chapter 15 recognition hearing is set for May 20. The Republic needs the US court to recognize the local-law exchange as a 'foreign proceeding' and grant the automatic stay under Section 362. The holdouts have retained counsel (specializing in sovereign litigation) and will likely argue that the local-law exchange was coercive (the 93% participation included regulatory pressure on domestic banks). The Republic's US counsel cites the NML v. Argentina precedent: the Second Circuit upheld the validity of a local-law exchange under New York law. But the aggregation clause here is governed by English law (the bonds are English-law, not NY-law). The English High Court's decision in Assenagon v. Republic of Congo on single-limb aggregation is the leading authority — it upheld the aggregation but required the issuer to act 'in good faith and for a proper purpose.'

Decision framework for the May 15 board meeting: (1) Exercise single-limb aggregation if the 2025s trustee confirms participation by May 10. (2) If the 2025s abstain, consider a 'exit consent' amendment to strip the CACs from the 2029s and 2034s — requires 50% per series. Current participation on those series is 62% and 68% respectively, so exit consent is feasible. Risk: exit consent litigation (Elliott v. Peru precedent) and potential pari passu challenges. (3) Parallel track: negotiate with the holdout group on a 'sweetener' — additional 2% principal recovery (cost: ~€17M) in exchange for their support. The IMF staff has signaled this would be acceptable if it ensures timely completion. The Chapter 15 recognition order is needed by June 30 to avoid a technical default on the IMF program's structural benchmark. The DIP financing equivalent (the Fund's disbursement) is conditional on the restructuring being 'effectively completed.'

judge_reason: The discussion concerns a sovereign debt restructuring, IMF program conditionality, and potential technical default, all of which have major financial and legal consequences for a country and its creditors.

Board Resolution Committee — Confidential

Item 4: 165(d) Resolution Plan — Material Entity Mapping & MREL Calibration

Per the 2024 guidance, we need to re-segment the US IHC's material entities (MEs) under the single-point-of-entry (SPOE) strategy. Current mapping shows 7 MEs; the Federal Reserve's horizontal review flagged 3 for insufficient separability analysis (ME-2, ME-4, ME-7).

Action items:
- Re-run the separability scoring model with updated shared-services cost allocations (IT, risk, treasury) per Appendix B.
- Recalibrate internal MREL for each ME using the new loss-absorption capacity (LAC) haircuts — 8% for op-risk, 12% for market-risk, 15% for counterparty credit risk.
- Prepare the operational continuity workbook for the March 31 submission. Focus on critical shared services (CCP access, payment systems, liquidity facilities) and the 72-hour playbook.

Please confirm the revised ME list and LAC tables by COB Friday. Legal needs final sign-off on the inter-affiliate agreements (IAAs) before the April 15 filing window.

Acknowledged. I'll have the separability model re-run with the updated cost pools by Thursday EOD. The shared-services allocation methodology (Step 3 of Appendix B) shifts ~$420M of treasury and funding costs across MEs — this moves ME-4 above the materiality threshold (5% of consolidated RWAs) and ME-7 below it. I'll flag the threshold crossing in the commentary.

On MREL: the new LAC haircuts increase total internal MREL requirement by ~€1.8B equivalent. ME-2 absorbs the largest share given its derivative clearing exposure. I'll circulate the revised LAC tables with the waterfall allocation (senior unsecured → sub debt → preferred → CET1) for each ME.

Operational continuity workbook: the 72-hour playbook for CCP access (DTCC, LCH, CME) and Fedwire/FedNow connectivity is drafted. Key dependency is the shared treasury platform — failover to the secondary data center adds 4 hours. I'll include the mitigant (pre-positioned liquidity at each ME).

IAAs: Legal's mark-up on the cross-ME funding and loss-sharing provisions is under review. The netting and set-off clauses need alignment with the updated ISDA 2021 Resolution Stay Protocol adherence letters. Targeting Friday noon for final package.

Good. On the ME-4/ME-7 threshold shift — document the rationale clearly for the horizontal review team. They'll probe the cost allocation methodology. Use the 'proportional usage' basis per SR 19-17, not the legacy 'headcount' basis.

Also, confirm the MREL calibration reflects the January 2024 final rule on TLAC holdings (deduction for investments in other MEs' TLAC). The double-counting adjustment reduces the group's external MREL need by ~$600M but increases internal allocation complexity.

One more item: the resolvability assessment framework (RAF) scoring. The Fed's 2024 RAF feedback letter rated 'Governance' and 'Operational Continuity' as 'Needs Improvement.' We need specific remediation milestones with owners and dates in the submission. Assign leads by Monday.

Noted on SR 19-17 proportional usage — will re-base the allocation and include the methodology memo as Appendix B-1. The headcount-to-usage shift reduces ME-4's allocated shared-services cost by ~$85M but increases ME-2's by ~$110M (higher derivative trade volume). Net effect on ME-4 materiality is marginal; I'll show the sensitivity.

TLAC holdings deduction: confirmed. The $600M external MREL reduction flows through the group-level calibration. Internal MREL allocation uses the 'waterfall with subordination' approach per the final rule — each ME's senior unsecured capacity is tested first, then sub debt, then preferred. I'll add a reconciliation schedule showing group external MREL → internal MREL by ME → LAC composition.

RAF remediation:
- Governance: Enhanced board resolution committee charter (draft by 3/15, approval 3/29), ME-level resolution management committees (charters by 3/22).
- Operational Continuity: Critical shared services mapping v2.0 (3/18), 72-hour playbook tabletop exercise (4/10), failover test for treasury platform (4/24).

Owners assigned. Will compile the RAF remediation tracker with milestones, owners, and evidence requirements for Monday's review.

Actuarial Memorandum — Confidential

Re: Run-off Portfolio Solvency Assessment — LifeCo Reinsurance Treaty X-997

Valuation date: 12/31/2023. Treaty covers 1985-2005 cohort of guaranteed minimum death benefit (GMDB) and guaranteed minimum income benefit (GMIB) variable annuity riders. Current in-force: 42,317 policies, $18.7B account value, $2.3B guaranteed value.

Key assumptions update:
- Mortality: 2012 IAM Basic with 15-year selection factors, mortality improvement Scale MP-2021.
- Lapse: Dynamic formula (shock lapse at 125% moneyness, base 2.5% ultimate).
- Utilization: GMIB take-up 85% at first eligibility, GMDB 100%.
- Interest rates: Treasury curve + 45bp illiquidity premium, mean reversion 3.5% UFR.
- Equity: 8.0% expected return, 18% vol, -0.35 correlation to rates.

Stochastic results (10,000 scenarios):
- CTE(90) statutory reserves: $1.42B
- CTE(95) economic reserves: $1.68B
- Available capital (post-dividend): $1.55B
- RBC ratio: 382% (company action level 200%)

Concern: The CTE(95) economic reserve exceeds available capital by $130M under current assumptions. Sensitivity to lapse assumption (shock lapse at 115% moneyness) adds $220M to CTE(95).

Request: Review the assumption governance process and confirm if a management action (reinsurance recapture, hedge restructuring, or capital contribution) is required before the 3/31 statutory filing.

Reviewed the stochastic output and assumption set. Several items:

1. Mortality improvement: MP-2021 vs. MP-2023 adds ~$45M to CTE(95). Recommend updating to MP-2023 for consistency with VM-21 guidance. The 15-year selection period is appropriate for the 1985-2005 cohort.

2. Lapse shock at 125% moneyness: The 115% sensitivity is a valid stress. However, the dynamic formula's moneyness calculation uses the *current* account value vs. guaranteed value — this ignores the path-dependency of ratchet/step-up features. A path-dependent lapse model (scenario-by-scenario) would increase CTE(95) by an estimated $60-80M. Suggest adding as a qualitative disclosure.

3. Utilization: 85% GMIB take-up assumes rational behavior. Behavioral economics literature suggests 90-95% for deep-in-the-money riders. At 95%, CTE(95) increases ~$90M.

4. Hedge program: The current delta/gamma overlay covers 65% of GMDB/GMIB Greeks. The residual tail risk (equity down 30% + rates down 100bp) drives the CTE(95) capital shortfall. A dynamic hedging overlay (variance swaps, OTM puts) could reduce CTE(95) by ~$180M at ~15bps annual cost.

5. Reinsurance: Treaty X-997 is 90% coinsurance with a $500M trust. Recapture would release the trust but increase statutory reserves by the ceded amount (~$1.1B CTE(90)). Not recommended unless capital contribution is available.

Recommendation: Proceed with hedge restructuring (item 4) and capital contribution of $150M (parent surplus note, 5-year, 6.5%). This closes the CTE(95) gap with margin. Update assumptions to MP-2023 and document lapse/utilization sensitivities in the Actuarial Opinion. Target 3/20 for revised run.

Agreed on hedge restructuring and capital contribution. The parent surplus note terms: 5-year, 6.5%, non-cumulative interest deferral option, sub to policyholder claims. Legal to draft by 3/10.

On assumption governance: The MP-2023 update and path-dependent lapse sensitivity will be documented in the Assumption Change Memo (ACM-2024-03). The Valuation Actuary signs off; CRO and CFO countersign per the Assumption Governance Policy (v4.2, Section 7.3).

One additional item: The treaty's experience refund provision (Article 12) triggers at 110% loss ratio on a rolling 5-year basis. Current projected loss ratio: 108%. A 50bps increase in equity vol or 20bps decrease in UFR pushes it over 110%, requiring a $45M refund to the ceding company. Model this as a contingent liability in the economic balance sheet.

Also: The RBC C-3 Phase II interest rate risk charge uses the 'standard scenario' (rates down 200bps). Under the proposed VM-22 reform, the 'severe scenario' (rates down 300bps + equity down 35%) would increase the C-3 charge by ~$340M. Run this as a pro forma for the ORSA.

Final package due 3/25 for Audit Committee review. Statutory filing 3/31.

Confirmed. ACM-2024-03 will include:
- MP-2023 update: +$45M CTE(95)
- Path-dependent lapse sensitivity: +$60-80M (qualitative)
- Utilization 95% sensitivity: +$90M
- Experience refund contingent liability: $45M at 110% loss ratio trigger
- VM-22 pro forma C-3 Phase II severe scenario: +$340M RBC charge

Hedge restructuring: Variance swap overlay (5-year, 10% vega notional) + 10% OTM put ladder (quarterly rolls). Estimated cost 14.5bps/yr on $18.7B AV. CTE(95) reduction ~$180M. Counterparty: AA-rated dealer, CSA with $15M threshold.

Capital contribution: $150M surplus note, 5Y, 6.5%, non-cumulative deferral, sub to policyholders. Legal draft by 3/10, execution by 3/22.

Economic balance sheet adjustment: Add $45M contingent liability for experience refund. Available capital post-adjustment: $1.505B. CTE(95) economic reserve (with hedge): ~$1.50B. Margin: ~$5M — thin but acceptable with management actions documented.

ORSA pro forma: VM-22 severe scenario C-3 charge +$340M → RBC ratio drops to ~310%. Still well above 200% CAL. Will include in ORSA report Section 4.3.

Audit Committee package: Revised stochastic run, ACM-2024-03, hedge term sheet, surplus note term sheet, ORSA pro forma. Target 3/25 delivery. Statutory filing 3/31 with Actuarial Opinion referencing all assumption changes and management actions.

Restructuring Committee — Weekly Status

Portfolio Company: Atlas Industrial Holdings (AIH)
Facility: $1.2B LBO (2021) — $750M TLB, $250M Revolver, $200M 2L
Current: TLB trading 82-84, 2L trading 55-60. LTM EBITDA $145M (vs. $195M at close). Net leverage 6.8x (covenant 5.5x springing at 90% revolver usage).

Covenant breach timeline:
- Q4'23: Springing leverage covenant tested at 6.2x (breach). 30-day cure period expired 1/15/24.
- Q1'24: Minimum liquidity covenant ($50M) — current $38M cash + $45M undrawn revolver (lender block at 90%).
- Cross-default: 2L indenture cross-default triggered at 60 days post-TLB event of default (3/16/24).

RSA status: Ad hoc group (holding 65% TLB, 70% 2L) engaged. Term sheet circulated 2/20:
- Debt-for-equity: $900M TLB/2L → 92% Newco equity
- $300M new money TLB (superpriority, 3Y, SOFR+650, 1% floor)
- Management roll: 8% Newco equity (vesting 4Y)
- Warrants: 5% to ad hoc group (strike $0.01)
- Releases: Customary, carve-out for fraud/gross negligence

DIP: $150M superpriority (SOFR+500, 18M) committed by ad hoc group. Budget weeks 1-13 attached.

Chapter 11 filing target: 3/25 (pre-cross-default). RSA execution target: 3/15.

Open items: Pension liability ($85M PBGC claim), environmental (EPA Superfund site — $40M estimate), intercompany claims ($220M).

Please review RSA term sheet and DIP budget. Confirm lender group consent solicitation timeline.

Reviewed RSA term sheet and DIP budget. Comments:

1. Valuation: The $900M debt-for-equity implies ~$978M enterprise value (including $300M new money, $85M pension, $40M environmental, $220M intercompany). At 6.7x LTM EBITDA ($145M), this is a 15% discount to the 7.9x comp set. The ad hoc group's 92% equity + warrants implies a 97% recovery on their $975M claim (TLB + 2L). TLB-only holders (35% non-participating) get ~85% recovery via new TLB — reasonable.

2. New money TLB: $300M at SOFR+650 is tight. DIP at SOFR+500 rolls into exit financing? Need clarity on takeout. Suggest adding a 101 soft call after 12 months.

3. Pension: $85M PBGC claim is Section 4062 liability. In Chapter 11, PBGC gets administrative expense priority for post-petition contributions, but pre-petition is general unsecured. The RSA treats it as general unsecured — correct. However, PBGC may assert 'substantial cessation' liability (~$120M). Need PBGC agreement pre-filing.

4. Environmental: $40M is the low end. EPA's PRP allocation for the Superfund site ranges $40-120M. The RSA should include an environmental escrow ($60M) funded from new money, with reopener if final allocation >$60M.

5. Intercompany: $220M claim by SponsorCo (shareholder loans + management fees). Subordination per the intercreditor agreement? The 2L indenture subordinates shareholder loans. Confirm SponsorCo votes per the RSA (they hold 15% TLB).

6. DIP budget: Weeks 1-13 shows $150M usage. Critical vendor payments ($22M), payroll ($18M), environmental remediation ($8M), professional fees ($35M). Adequate but tight. Add $10M contingency.

Consent solicitation: Need 66.67% TLB and 50.1% 2L for RSA amendments. Ad hoc group has 65%/70%. Solicitation launch 3/1, deadline 3/14. Non-participating TLB holders (35%) likely object — prepare for contested hearing.

Filing timeline: 3/25 is aggressive. RSA execution 3/15, consent results 3/14, first day motions 3/25. Confirm court availability (Delaware).

Good catch on the environmental escrow and PBGC substantial cessation. Updates:

- Environmental escrow: $60M from new money TLB proceeds, reopener at final EPA allocation. Escrow agent: Wilmington Trust.
- PBGC: Engage PBGC counsel this week. Target agreement on $85M general unsecured treatment + $15M administrative expense for post-petition contributions. If 'substantial cessation' asserted, cap at $120M total.
- Intercompany: SponsorCo's 15% TLB votes *with* ad hoc group per the RSA support agreement. The $220M shareholder loan is contractually subordinated (2L indenture Section 10.4). SponsorCo's recovery: 8% management roll equity only.
- New money TLB: Added 101 soft call at 12 months. Takeout: Refinance at exit via ABL ($200M) + new 2L ($100M) — term sheet from incumbent agent bank attached.
- DIP: Added $10M contingency. Total $160M. Ad hoc group commits $160M (pro rata).

Consent solicitation: Launch 3/1. Materials: RSA, DIP order, disclosure statement summary. Solicitation agent: Georgeson. Deadline 3/14, 5 PM ET.

Contested hearing prep: Non-participating TLB holders (Oaktree, GSO — ~22% combined) likely argue 'unfair discrimination' (TLB vs 2L recovery differential). Defense: Valuation expert (Houlihan Lokey) shows 2L recovery 55% vs TLB 85% is consistent with priority. Waterfall analysis attached.

Chapter 11 venue: Delaware confirmed. Judge Dorsey assigned. First day hearings 3/26 (DIP, cash management, critical vendors).

Action items:
- PBGC engagement: by 3/5
- Environmental escrow agreement: by 3/8
- Consent solicitation launch: 3/1
- RSA execution: 3/15
- Filing: 3/25

Circulate updated RSA (v3), DIP budget v2, and consent materials by EOD tomorrow.

Updated RSA v3, DIP budget v2, and consent materials circulated. Key changes in RSA v3:
- Environmental escrow $60M (Section 4.7)
- PBGC treatment: $85M GUC + $15M admin + $20M cessation cap (Section 4.8)
- New money TLB: 101 soft call at 12M (Section 3.2)
- Exit financing commitment letter attached as Exhibit F
- Release carve-out: Added 'willful misconduct' alongside fraud/gross negligence (Section 12.3)

DIP budget v2: $160M total. Added $10M contingency (Line 47). Professional fees updated to $38M (added PBGC counsel $1.5M, environmental counsel $1M).

Consent solicitation package: RSA v3, DIP budget v2, disclosure statement summary (15 pages), valuation summary (Houlihan Lokey), waterfall analysis, FAQ. Georgeson to distribute 3/1 8 AM ET.

Houlihan Lokey valuation: EV range $920-1,040M. Midpoint $980M supports RSA allocation. Waterfall:
- Superpriority DIP: $160M (100%)
- Admin/Priority: $45M (100%)
- TLB (participating): $650M → 92% Newco equity (97% recovery)
- 2L (participating): $140M → 92% Newco equity (97% recovery)
- TLB (non-participating): $100M → New TLB $85M (85% recovery)
- 2L (non-participating): $60M → GUC recovery ~15%

messages.content:
Joint Defense Group — Privileged & Confidential

Re: In re: National Prescription Opioid Litigation — MDL No. 2804
Discovery Sanctions Motion — Defendant Manufacturer's Response Due 3/22

Plaintiffs' Motion for Sanctions (Doc. 14,892) alleges:
- Spoliation: Failure to preserve 1.2M documents from 'Project Horizon' (2015-2018 marketing analytics platform). Auto-deletion protocol activated 2019 despite litigation hold (2017).
- False certifications: Rule 26(g) certifications (2018-2021) stated 'all responsive documents produced.' Forensic review shows 340K emails withheld.
- Witness coaching: Deposition prep materials for Dr. K. (former CMO) show scripted responses re: 'addiction risk minimization.'

Sanctions sought: Adverse inference jury instruction, preclusion of defense experts, $25M monetary sanctions, referral to DOJ.

Our position:
- Project Horizon: Platform migrated to cloud 2019. Auto-deletion was system-wide (90-day retention), not targeted. Litigation hold notice sent 2017 — IT acknowledges gap in hold implementation for legacy analytics data. Not intentional.
- Rule 26(g): Certifications based on reasonable inquiry at the time. Supplemental productions 2022-2023 (4.2M docs) cured deficiencies.
- Witness coaching: Prep materials reflect standard witness preparation. No evidence of suborned perjury.

Need: Response brief outline by 3/8. Expert report (digital forensics) by 3/15. Declaration from IT Director (hold implementation) by 3/10.

Key cases: Zubulake IV (spoliation factors), Chin v. Port of Seattle (proportionality), Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(e) (intent requirement).

Judge Polster's standing order: 'Sanctions motions will be heard on the papers unless oral argument requested.' No oral argument scheduled.

Please assign drafting leads.

Assignments:
- Response brief lead: Sarah C. (associate, e-discovery background). Outline by 3/8, draft by 3/15, final by 3/20.
- Digital forensics expert: Retain Stroz Friedberg. Scope: (1) Project Horizon architecture & auto-deletion logic, (2) litigation hold notice dissemination & IT acknowledgment logs, (3) forensic recovery of deleted data from backups/cloud snapshots. Report by 3/15.
- IT Director declaration: Michael T. (VP Infrastructure). Draft by 3/8, review by 3/10, execute by 3/12. Content: Hold notice receipt 2017, gap in legacy analytics coverage, 2019 migration project scope, no intentional deletion.
- Witness coaching defense: Mark R. (partner). Deposition prep materials review — distinguish preparation from coaching. Affidavit from Dr. K. counsel (outside litigation counsel) by 3/12.

Legal framework:
- Rule 37(e): Sanctions only if 'intent to deprive.' Our evidence: systemic auto-deletion, not targeted. Zubulake factor 3 (culpability) — negligence at most.
- Rule 26(g): 'Reasonable inquiry' standard. Supplemental productions demonstrate good faith.
- Inherent authority: Requires bad faith. Chin v. Port of Seattle — proportionality limits sanctions to prejudice caused.

Prejudice analysis: Plaintiffs received 4.2M supplemental docs 2022-2023. Project Horizon data: marketing analytics, not clinical/safety. Key custodians (CMO, VP Sales) produced emails separately. Prejudice minimal.

Monetary sanctions: $25M is disproportionate. Cost to reproduce: ~$200K (forensic recovery). Fees incurred: ~$1.2M. Will argue for cost-shifting only.

DOJ referral: No basis. No evidence of criminal contempt or fraud on court.

Strategy: File response 3/22 with expert report, IT declaration, Dr. K. counsel affidavit. Request evidentiary hearing if Court inclined to grant adverse inference.

Budget: Stroz Friedberg ~$180K. Outside counsel for Dr. K. ~$75K. Total incremental ~$255K.

Please confirm assignments and budget.

Confirmed. Budget approved.

Additional items:

1. The 'Project Horizon' data includes geotargeted marketing spend by ZIP code correlated with prescribing data (IQVIA). This *is* relevant to plaintiffs' 'targeted marketing' theory. The forensic expert must address recoverability of this specific dataset. If unrecoverable, quantify the prejudice — but argue alternative sources (IQVIA direct purchase, CMS data, state PDMP) mitigate.

2. Rule 26(g) certifications: The 2018-2021 certifications were signed by outside counsel (not in-house). Outside counsel's reasonable inquiry relied on IT's representation that 'all custodial emails collected.' IT's representation was incomplete (legacy analytics excluded). This is a *counsel reliance* defense — document the communication chain.

3. Judge Polster's prior rulings in MDL 2804: He denied adverse inference in *City of Cleveland v. Purdue* (2022) for similar auto-deletion (negligence, not intent). He granted monetary sanctions ($500K) for costs. Cite heavily.

4. The ad hoc 'State AG' group (22 states) filed a joinder to the sanctions motion. Their brief emphasizes 'pattern of obstruction' across MDL defendants. Our response must distinguish: no prior sanctions orders against this defendant. Clean record.

5. Settlement context: Global settlement framework (Exhibit G to the Master Settlement Agreement) requires 'full discovery compliance.' A sanctions order with adverse inference *could* trigger a settlement compliance dispute. Flag for settlement team.

Revised timeline:
- 3/5: Stroz Friedberg kickoff
- 3/8: Response outline + IT declaration draft + counsel reliance memo
- 3/12: Dr. K. counsel affidavit
- 3/15: Stroz report (preliminary)
- 3/18: Response brief draft
- 3/20: Final review
- 3/22: Filing

Settlement team sync: 3/6. Please coordinate.

All items incorporated. Revised assignments:

1. Geotargeted marketing/IQVIA correlation: Stroz scope expanded. They'll attempt recovery from: (a) AWS S3 versioning (Project Horizon migrated to S3 2018), (b) Snowflake time travel (analytics warehouse, 90-day), (c) IQVIA direct data purchase (budget $50K). If unrecoverable, prejudice memo: alternative sources cover 85% of ZIP-code/prescribing correlation (CMS Part D, state PDMP, IQVIA LRx).

2. Counsel reliance chain: Documented. Outside counsel (Williams & Connolly) email 1/15/2018 to IT: 'Confirm all custodial email sources collected for litigation hold.' IT response 1/18/2018: 'Confirmed — Exchange, O365, legacy PSTs.' Legacy analytics (Project Horizon) not mentioned. Follow-up 2020: IT disclosed gap. Will attach email chain as Exhibit C to IT declaration.

3. *City of Cleveland* cite: Confirmed. Polster J. denied adverse inference, granted $500K costs. Key language: 'Negligent failure to preserve, without more, does not satisfy Rule 37(e)'s intent requirement.' Will lead with this.

4. State AG joinder: Response will include 'clean record' section — no prior sanctions, no spoliation findings, 4.2M supplemental docs produced voluntarily. Distinguish from defendants with prior adverse rulings (Endo, Mallinckrodt).

5. Settlement compliance: Flagged. Settlement team (Kevin M.) added to distribution. Sync 3/6 2 PM ET.

Stroz kickoff 3/5 10 AM ET. Preliminary findings call 3/12. Final report 3/15.

Response brief structure:
I. Introduction: No intent, minimal prejudice, clean record
II. Project Horizon: Systemic auto-deletion, not targeted; recoverability analysis
III. Rule 26(g): Counsel reliance, supplemental productions cure
IV. Witness coaching: Standard preparation, no subornation
V. Sanctions analysis: Rule 37(e) intent, Zubulake factors, Chin proportionality, *Cleveland* precedent
VI. Requested relief: Deny adverse inference/preclusion; limit monetary to cost-shifting (~$1.4M); deny DOJ referral

Drafting on track. Daily standups 9 AM ET through filing.

messages.content:
Sovereign Debt Restructuring — Technical Committee

Country: Republic of Verona (pseudonym)
Debt Stock: $42.3B external (Eurobonds $28.1B, bilateral $9.2B, multilateral $5.0B)
Eurobonds: 12 series, 2025-2042 maturities, CACs (single-limb, 75%/66.67%), governing law: English/NY
Bilateral: Paris Club (pre-2020) + non-Paris Club (China EXIM $3.8B, India $1.2B, Gulf $2.1B)
Multilateral: IMF ($2.1B EFF), World Bank ($1.8B), AfDB ($1.1B) — preferred creditor status

DSA (Debt Sustainability Analysis) — IMF Staff Report 2024:
- PV of debt-to-GDP: 78% (threshold 70%)
- PV of debt-to-exports: 210% (threshold 180%)
- Debt service-to-revenue: 38% (threshold 22%)
- Gross financing need: 14% of GDP (3-year avg)

Baseline: Unsustainable. Restructuring needed to restore sustainability with high probability.

Perimeter: Eurobonds only (commercial creditors). Bilateral/multilateral treated per comparable treatment.

Proposed restructuring envelope (IMF program baseline):
- Principal haircut: 25% (NPV basis)
- Maturity extension: +7 years (weighted avg)
- Coupon reduction: 150bps (weighted avg)
- NPV reduction: ~32% (at 9% exit yield)

CAC mechanics: Single-limb aggregation across all 12 series. 75% voting threshold per series, 66.67% aggregated. Holdout risk: 3 series have <75% per-series ownership by coordinating group.

Comparable treatment: Paris Club — flow rescheduling on Houston terms (maturity extension only, no haircut). Non-Paris Club — case-by-case. China EXIM: historically prefers maturity extension + grace period.

IMF program: 36-month EFF, $2.1B. Prior actions: (1) Revenue measures (VAT +2%, excise), (2) Expenditure rationalization (subsidy reform), (3) Restructuring launch by 6/30.

Timeline:
- 3/15: Creditor committee formation (ad hoc group target: 50%+ Eurobond holding)
- 4/15: Term sheet exchange
- 5/15: Consent solicitation launch
- 6/30: Implementation (exchange offer + consent solicitation)

Open items: Exit yield assumption (9% vs. current 11.5%), GDP-linked warrant structure, collective action clause aggregation across governing laws (English vs. NY), China EXIM engagement.

Please review DSA assumptions and restructuring envelope. Confirm creditor committee outreach strategy.

Reviewed DSA and restructuring envelope. Comments:

1. Exit yield: 9% is optimistic. Current Eurobond curve: 2025s 11.5%, 2030s 10.8%, 2040s 10.2%. A 9% exit yield implies significant spread compression post-restructuring (current spread ~750bps over UST). Suggest 10% base case, 9% upside. At 10%, NPV reduction drops to ~26% — may not meet IMF 'restore sustainability with high probability' standard. Need deeper haircut or longer extension.

2. GDP-linked warrants: Standard structure — notional = 5% of restructured principal, kick-in at 3% real GDP growth, cap at 1.5x notional, maturity 2045. Adds ~3% NPV recovery for creditors at 10% exit yield. Helps bridge the 26%→32% gap. Recommend inclusion.

3. CAC aggregation: English law bonds (8 series, $19.2B) and NY law bonds (4 series, $8.9B) have *different* CAC thresholds (75%/66.67% vs. 75%/66.67% — same thresholds but separate aggregation). Single-limb *across* governing laws requires a scheme of arrangement (UK) or Chapter 15 (US) to bind holdouts cross-border. Alternative: Parallel consent solicitations with 'pooling' mechanism. Recommend UK Scheme of Arrangement for English law bonds (binds 75% per class) + NY law consent solicitation (66.67% per series). Cross-border recognition via Chapter 15.

4. China EXIM: $3.8B across 7 loans (2016-2022). Preferred structure: 20-year maturity, 10-year grace, 2% fixed coupon. No haircut. NPV reduction ~35% at 9% discount rate — comparable to commercial creditor NPV haircut. Engage via Paris Club co-chairs (France/UK). Timeline: Paris Club meeting 4/20.

5. Creditor committee: Target ad hoc group formation by 3/15. Key holders: BlackRock ($2.1B), Amundi ($1.8B), PIMCO ($1.5B), Ashmore ($1.2B), T. Rowe ($900M). Combined ~$7.5B (27%). Need additional $3B+ for 50%+. Outreach to hedge funds (Greylock, Gramercy, Redwood) — estimated $2.5B combined.

6. DSA sensitivity: Stress test — growth -1%, primary balance -1% GDP, exchange rate -10%. PV debt-to-GDP rises to 92%. Restructuring envelope must withstand stress. Suggest contingent capital instrument (CCI) — triggers additional 5% haircut if debt-to-GDP >85% at 2027 review.

- Principal haircut: 28%
- Maturity extension: +8 years
- Coupon reduction: 175bps
- GDP warrants: 5% notional, 3% trigger, 1.5x cap
- CCI: 5% additional haircut trigger at 85% debt-to-GDP (2027)
- NPV reduction: ~34% at 10% exit yield

Please confirm revised envelope and legal structure (UK Scheme + NY consent + Chapter 15).

UK Scheme: Class composition — each of 8 English law series = separate class (same voting rights). 75% value per class. Scheme meeting 6/15, Court sanction hearing 6/25. Sanction binds all creditors in each class (including holdouts).

NY law bonds: Consent solicitation per series. 66.67% per series. No cross-series aggregation. Exchange offer for non-consenting holders (same terms).

GDP warrants: Draft term sheet attached. Issuer: Republic of Verona. Notional: 5% of restructured principal ($1.4B). Trigger: Real GDP growth >3% (IMF WEO data). Payment: 0.5% of notional per 0.5% growth above trigger, capped at 1.5x. Maturity: 2045. Governing law: English.

CCI: Contingent Capital Instrument. Trigger: PV debt-to-GDP >85% at 2027 DSA review (IMF staff report). Mechanism: Additional 5% principal haircut via mandatory exchange into new series (2035 maturity, 0% coupon). Governing law: English.
